nameStory: The American kestrel gets its name from the Old French word 'crecerelle,' which referred to a small falcon that made a harsh, rattling call. You might sometimes hear it called a 'sparrowhawk,' but that's actually a misnomer - this bird is a true falcon, not a hawk at all!
description: The American kestrel is North America's smallest and most common falcon, about the size of a blue jay to mourning dove depending on sex and subspecies. These colorful little raptors sport beautiful rufous (reddish-brown) backs with distinctive dark barring, and females are noticeably larger than males. Unlike many birds, young kestrels look remarkably similar to their parents, making identification easier year-round. Their compact, streamlined falcon body and pointed wings make them unmistakable once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Size and Proportions
idTips.description: Small falcon with a compact body, roughly blue jay to mourning dove sized, with long pointed wings and a relatively long tail for a falcon

idTips.label: Rufous Back Pattern
idTips.description: Rich reddish-brown back with bold dark bars running across it - looks almost brick-colored in good light

idTips.label: Hovering Behavior
idTips.description: Often hovers in place with rapid, fluttering wingbeats while hunting - like a tiny helicopter scanning the ground below

idTips.label: Perching Posture
idTips.description: Sits upright on fence posts, power lines, and dead snags with alert, erect posture - head often turning sharply to scan for prey

idTips.label: Facial Pattern
idTips.description: Distinctive facial markings with dark 'mustache' stripes and white cheeks - gives them an almost painted look

habitat: American kestrels thrive in New England's open and semi-open landscapes including farmland, meadows, grasslands, and field edges with scattered trees or fence posts for perching. They favor areas where short grass or mowed fields provide good hunting visibility for grasshoppers, mice, and small birds. You'll often spot them along rural roads, in agricultural areas, and near airports or large park openings.

seasonality.spring: Breeding pairs arrive and become very vocal, often seen courtship flying and hunting actively in open areas. This is when you'll hear their distinctive 'killy-killy-killy' calls most frequently.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity as parents hunt constantly to feed nestlings in tree cavities or nest boxes. Young birds learning to hunt may appear clumsy and vocal.
seasonality.fall: Migration brings increased numbers through New England, with birds often seen hunting along highways and in harvested agricultural fields.
seasonality.winter: Some birds remain year-round in southern New England, becoming more dependent on small mammals and birds as insects become scarce.

funFact: American kestrels are natural pest controllers - a single bird can eat over 300 grasshoppers in a day during peak summer hunting, making them worth their weight in gold to farmers and gardeners!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Sharp-shinned Hawks, but kestrels have pointed falcon wings (not rounded hawk wings), hover frequently, and show that distinctive rufous back coloring. Memory trick: 'Kestrels hover, hawks don't' - if you see a small raptor hovering like a hummingbird, it's likely a kestrel.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sparrowhawk' in some regions, American kestrels are true falcons, not hawks. This naming confusion stems from their small size and bird-hunting habits, but their pointed wings, flight style, and family relationships clearly place them with other falcons like Peregrines and Merlins.
compareHints: Among New England's falcons, American kestrels are by far the smallest and most colorful, with that distinctive rufous back that neither Merlins nor Peregrine Falcons possess. Merlins are stockier and darker overall, while Peregrine Falcons are much larger and show more uniform gray-blue coloring above.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to American Kestrels, merlins are stockier with less colorful plumage and never hover while hunting.
Peregrine Falcons are much larger than American Kestrels (which are robin-sized with rusty coloring) and Merlins (which are jay-sized and heavily streaked).

Compared to its falcon relatives in New England, the gyrfalcon dwarfs the robin-sized American kestrel and pigeon-sized merlin, while being noticeably bulkier and broader-winged than the peregrine falcon.
Unlike American Kestrels which show rusty-red backs and tails, Red-footed Falcons are much grayer overall with those distinctive bright red legs.
Among New England's falcons, prairie falcons are most similar to peregrine falcons in size and hunting style, but are much paler with sandy-brown tones instead of blue-gray.
